    Exactly. Now I have the programming philosophy, not just the mechanics.

    What you're describing is essentially a top-down, job-oriented development method with the architecture established before the individual code is written.

    The workflow we were establishing is:

    1. Define the Job.
      Start with the actual end-to-end Job the prototype must accomplish—not a tiny piece of it.

    2. Ask Chappy to decompose the Job.
      Determine how many distinct tasks are required to accomplish the Job.

    3. Make each task a subroutine.
      Each subroutine has one responsibility. It performs its task and, importantly, verifies that the task was actually completed rather than simply assuming success.

    4. Establish the task map.
      Once the tasks are known, we know the architecture of the program before we start filling in the details.

    5. Write the Head Program first.
      The Head Program is the Task Clock / Hub / Orchestrator. It establishes the sequence and controls when each task is called. At this stage, we're defining the skeleton of the Job, not trying to bury all the actual work inside the head program.

    6. Write the subroutines afterward.
      Each routine is developed independently according to the task assigned to it.

    7. Each routine reports completion/status back to the Head Program.
      The Head Program then decides what task happens next, whether something needs to be repeated, or whether the Job is complete.

    The key philosophy

    The important distinction is:

    We design the complete Job first, then write the program that coordinates it.

    We're deliberately not doing this:

    write simple program → test → add feature → modify main program → add another feature → restructure → break something → patch it → add another feature → ...

    That's the "programmer gets trapped in endless modifications" problem you're trying to eliminate.

    Instead, we're doing:

    JOB → TASKS → TASK MAP → HEAD PROGRAM → SUBROUTINES → VERIFICATION → COMPLETE JOB

    That means the Head Program is designed with knowledge of the whole Job from the beginning, even though the individual subroutines haven't been written yet.

    And there's another principle here that I think is important to preserve:

    The number of subroutines isn't determined by how easy the program is to write. It's determined by how many distinct tasks the Job actually requires.

    So if a Job needs 17 logically separate tasks, we don't artificially squeeze it into three routines just to make the program look "simple." Conversely, we don't create 40 routines when several operations genuinely belong to one task.

    I would call this our "Job-First Structured Programming Schema" unless we had already given it another name yesterday.

    So from here, if you give me the Job we were building, I should be able to start at the point where we left off: first identify the complete task/subroutine inventory, then establish the Head/Task Clock architecture before writing the individual routines.

    The corrected architecture

    Head Program / Task Clock

    • Knows the task sequence.

    • Knows which subroutine to call.

    • Starts/stops or advances the task cycle.

    • Receives a status/result from each subroutine.

    • Decides whether to advance, repeat, wait, or terminate.

    • Does not contain the business logic of the Job.

    • Does not need to understand what any individual task actually accomplishes.

    Subroutines

    • Know what their particular task is.

    • Perform that task.

    • Verify that the task was completed successfully.

    • Return a defined status to the Head Program.

    • Don't need to know the details of the other tasks.

    So conceptually:

                        ┌─────────────────────┐
                    │   HEAD PROGRAM      │
                    │    TASK CLOCK       │
                    │                     │
                    │  Orchestrates only  │
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │
          ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
          │                    │                    │
          ▼                    ▼                    ▼
     ┌─────────┐          ┌─────────┐          ┌─────────┐
     │ TASK 01 │          │ TASK 02 │          │ TASK 03 │
     │         │          │         │          │         │
     │ Do task │          │ Do task │          │ Do task │
     │ Verify  │          │ Verify  │          │ Verify  │
     └────┬────┘          └────┬────┘          └────┬────┘
          │                    │                    │
          └──────── STATUS ────┴──── STATUS ───────┘
                               │
                               ▼
                         HEAD PROGRAM

    And that gives us a particularly clean separation:

    The Head Program controls when.
    The subroutine controls what.
    The subroutine verifies whether.

    SUCCESS
FAILURE
RETRY
WAIT

    The meaning of the task belongs entirely to the task module.

    That also makes the architecture much more powerful for prototyping. We can replace TASK_03 with a completely different implementation—as long as it obeys the agreed interface—and the Head Program doesn't have to be rewritten.

    That's the philosophy I will use going forward.

WEB REPOSITORY

    And this makes troubleshooting much easier

    Suppose the finished system reports:

    [FAIL] Routine 09 — Verify Actual Webpage

    We don't have to stare at some enormous monolithic program and wonder where the failure originated.

    We know:

    01 ✓
02 ✓
03 ✓
04 ✓
05 ✓
06 ✓
07 ✓
08 ✓
09 ✗

    Therefore:

    • input acquisition worked

    • archival worked

    • Web preparation worked

    • Library publication worked

    • Library verification worked

    • Web publication worked

    • Web repository verification worked

    • the failure is in the publication-to-browser boundary

    That's an enormous debugging advantage.

    And because Routine 09 has a narrow contract, we know where to look.

    There's an even deeper benefit

    It means we can test routines individually.

    We don't necessarily have to run the entire pipeline every time we modify something.

    For example, Routine 04 can eventually have test cases like:

    Given:
    valid Edge HTML
    valid *_files folder

Expected:
    index.html exists
    *_files exists
    original HTML == index.html
    original remains untouched

    Then:

    Given:
    two HTML files

Expected:
    failure

    Or:

    Given:
    no *_files directory

Expected:
    failure

    Routine 09 can have its own tests:

    Given:
    valid published page

Expected:
    PAGE_URL established

    and:

    Given:
    HTTP 404

Expected:
    failure

    We can therefore troubleshoot the machine one module at a time.

    That is exactly the benefit you were originally aiming for.

    I would preserve one more thing from your original instinct

    We shouldn't let modularity become an excuse for modules to become gigantic.

    A routine should have one conceptual job.

    Not:

    09_VERIFY_WEBPAGE.sh

check URL
repair URL
check DNS
change repository settings
wait for Pages
fix HTML
create link
...

    Instead:

    09_VERIFY_WEBPAGE.sh

"Given PAGE_URL, establish that the published webpage
is actually retrievable."

    If we discover that something else is necessary, that's probably another module.

    That's how we prevent the million-line monster from slowly sneaking back in through 50-line modules that each secretly do ten jobs.

    So I think our architecture now has four major principles

    1. Modularity

    Each routine has one coherent responsibility.

    2. Contracts

    Each routine explicitly states what it promises to establish.

    3. Independent verification

    A later routine does not blindly trust an earlier routine's claim when independent evidence is available.

    4. Controlled destruction

    No destructive transition occurs until the contracts establishing safety have been fulfilled.

    And I'd add a fifth:

    5. Minimal coupling

    A routine should know as little as possible about the internal implementation of other routines.

    That last one is what turns your original modular idea into a genuine architectural principle.

    The resulting mental model

    I think we should eventually be able to draw the entire uploader like this:

                             HUB
                          │
                          │
             ┌────────────┼────────────┐
             │            │            │
             ▼            ▼            ▼
          ROUTINE       ROUTINE      ROUTINE
             │            │            │
             │   contract │            │
             └────────────┼────────────┘
                          │
                       STATE
                          │
                          ▼
                    NEXT ROUTINE

    The Hub is the orchestrator.

    The routines are workers with contracts.

    The filesystem/GitHub are systems of record/state.

    The verification routines are evidence producers.

    And the destructive routines are controlled state transitions.

    That's a much more mature architecture than simply "13 Bash scripts called in sequence."

    And I think this is exactly why your original program turned out so well: you made the right architectural decision before writing the code. We are now making those implicit decisions explicit so that the redesign can be even more disciplined.

    So I agree: let's rewrite the uploader before we build the wizard. The uploader becomes our architectural laboratory and our reference implementation. Once that is solid, the wizard gets built against something we actually trust.

    Yes. I think that vocabulary is actually an important improvement, because it gives us a hierarchy that matches what the software is doing.

    I would refine it slightly so that each word has a distinct architectural meaning:

    Proposed vocabulary

    Step → the smallest meaningful operation.

    A step should do one thing and have a clear success/failure result.

    Examples:

    • Verify that a directory exists.

    • Copy a session.

    • Calculate a checksum.

    • Create a Git commit.

    • Ask GitHub for a repository state.

    • Delete a particular temporary directory.

    A step should not secretly take responsibility for a larger part of the workflow.

    Task → a coherent group of steps that accomplishes one identifiable responsibility.

    For example:

    Task: Verify Library

    Its steps might be:

    1. Enter the Library repository.

    2. Confirm the session directory exists.

    3. Confirm the original HTML exists.

    4. Confirm the _files directory exists.

    5. Confirm the working tree is clean.

    6. Contact the remote.

    7. Compare the relevant commits.

    8. Return success.

    The task has a contract:

    "If I return success, the Library satisfies the conditions I promised to verify."

    That's stronger than merely saying "the commands ran."

    Routine → the executable module that implements a task.

    This is where I think your original modular-design idea becomes especially powerful.

    So:

    Routine 06
    │
    └── implements the Task:
            "Verify Library"

    The routine is therefore a replaceable module.

    If we later discover a better way to verify GitHub, we can rewrite Routine 06 without redesigning the entire system.

    Job → the complete business operation performed by the head program.

    For example:

    Job: Process One Edge Capture

    The job consists of the tasks:

    Receive
    ↓
Verify Input
    ↓
Archive
    ↓
Prepare Web
    ↓
Push Library
    ↓
Verify Library
    ↓
Push Web
    ↓
Verify Web Files
    ↓
Verify Published Webpage
    ↓
Create Library Link
    ↓
Verify Library Link
    ↓
Clean Archive
    ↓
Clean Thumb Drive

    And the Hub is the mechanism that orchestrates those tasks.

    But I think there is one more word we need

    I'd introduce Contract as a first-class architectural concept.

    Not as something that is executed, but as something that defines what a step, task, or routine promises.

    So we get:

    CONTRACT
    │
    ▼
STEP
    │
    ▼
TASK
    │
    ▼
ROUTINE
    │
    ▼
JOB
    │
    ▼
HUB

    Although I would actually describe the relationship slightly differently:

                        JOB
                     │
                     ▼
                    HUB
                     │
              orchestrates
                     │
                     ▼
                   TASKS
                     │
             implemented by
                     │
                     ▼
                 ROUTINES
                     │
                composed of
                     │
                     ▼
                  STEPS
                     │
               governed by
                     │
                     ▼
                CONTRACTS

    That gives us a pretty rich little architectural language.

    And this explains the "redundant" verification

    This is the thing I think we have discovered through building Routines 01–13.

    At first glance, this looks excessive:

    05 Push Library
06 Verify Library

07 Push Web
08 Verify Web Files

09 Verify Webpage

10 Create Library Link
11 Verify Library Link

    But under the contract philosophy, it makes perfect sense.

    Routine 05's contract is approximately:

    I attempted the Library push and Git reported success.

    Routine 06's contract is stronger:

    The Library repository now demonstrably contains the expected session and agrees with its remote Git state.

    Routine 07:

    I attempted the Web push and Git reported success.

    Routine 08:

    The Web repository demonstrably contains the expected publishing files and agrees with its remote Git state.

    Routine 09:

    A client can actually retrieve the published webpage.

    Those are different facts.

    Therefore they deserve different contracts.

    The apparent redundancy is actually layered verification.

    This also gives us a rule for rewriting the program

    I think our new architectural rule should be:

    A routine must never assume that another routine's success proves its own contract.

    It may rely on the input conditions established by an earlier routine, but it must independently establish whatever its own contract promises.

    That distinction is subtle but extremely valuable.

    For example, Routine 10 can legitimately say:

    PAGE_URL was supplied by Routine 09

    But it shouldn't merely assume:

    PAGE_URL must therefore be valid.

    Its own contract is:

    "I will create a Library navigation file containing the supplied verified destination."

    Then Routine 11 independently establishes:

    "That navigation file actually exists in the Library repository and contains the expected destination."

    That's the architecture becoming self-checking.

    And modularity becomes a formal principle

    Your original idea about troubleshooting is worth making an explicit rule:

    A change to one routine should require no change to unrelated routines unless the routine's contract changes.

    For example:

    Routine 06 — Verify Library

    could eventually change from Git-based verification to some more sophisticated verification mechanism.

    As long as it continues to satisfy the same contract:

    INPUT:
    SESSION_NAME

PROMISE:
    Library contains the expected preserved session
    and the remote state has been independently verified.

SUCCESS:
    Contract satisfied.

FAILURE:
    Contract not established.

    the Hub doesn't care how Routine 06 accomplished it.

    That's true modularity, rather than merely putting pieces of a giant script into separate files.

    I would therefore change our design terminology

    Instead of thinking:

    13 scripts that happen to execute in sequence

    I think we should think:

    ONE JOB
│
├── Task 01
│     └── Routine 01
│           └── Steps
│
├── Task 02
│     └── Routine 02
│           └── Steps
│
├── Task 03
│     └── Routine 03
│           └── Steps
│
...
│
└── Task 13
      └── Routine 13
            └── Steps

    with every level governed by explicit contracts.

    And the Hub becomes intentionally boring:

    perform Task 01
    │
    ├── success → perform Task 02
    └── failure → STOP

perform Task 02
    │
    ├── success → perform Task 03
    └── failure → STOP

...

    That's a feature, not a weakness.

    The Hub should orchestrate.
    The routines should perform.
    The steps should execute.
    The contracts should define success.

    That gives us a much better foundation for rewriting the upload program before we touch the wizard.

    And I think the rewrite should begin not by rewriting Bash, but by writing the contract for every routine first. Once those contracts are solid, the Bash becomes an implementation detail rather than the architecture itself.
